summary: This informational document defines a set of algorithms that can be used with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol described in RFC 9052. Together with RFC 9052 it obsoletes RFC 8152.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9053 lists algorithms that COSE messages can use for signatures, message authentication, encryption, and key distribution. It complements RFC 9052, which defines the message structures and processing rules.

subtitle: The initial signature, authentication, encryption, and key-management algorithms for COSE.

tldr.problem: COSE needs concrete algorithms and compact identifiers for signing, authenticating, encrypting, and distributing keys in CBOR messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies algorithm identifiers and use requirements for ECDSA, EdDSA, HMAC, AES-MAC, AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20/Poly1305, HKDF, AES Key Wrap, ECDH, and COSE key objects.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9053 supplies algorithms for the structures in RFC 9052. Together they obsolete RFC 8152; RFC 9053 is Informational and was updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 9053 is an Informational document that, together with RFC 9052, obsoletes RFC 8152. RFC 9053 has been updated by RFC 9864.

sections.title: How This Fits into COSE
sections.content:
Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is designed for small messages and implementations. CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) adds message security. RFC 9052 defines serialization structures and general procedures, while RFC 9053 provides an initial set of algorithms for those structures.

RFC 9053 was created by splitting RFC 8152. The algorithm-specific material moved into this document, while general structures and processing rules moved into RFC 9052. The two documents together obsolete RFC 8152.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 9052 describes how COSE messages are structured. This RFC lists cryptographic algorithms those messages can use, with identifiers carried in messages.

sections.title: Signatures and Message Authentication
sections.content:
The signature algorithms are ECDSA with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512, and EdDSA. ECDSA is defined for P-256, P-384, and P-521 curves, while EdDSA uses its pure form rather than HashEdDSA. The RFC recommends deterministic ECDSA to avoid relying on a fresh random value for each signature.

The message-authentication algorithms are HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512, and AES-CBC-MAC with specified key and tag sizes. Implementations must check that key type, key length, algorithm, and any key-operation restrictions match the operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can identify who signed a message, while a MAC checks that a message was not changed by someone without the key. The RFC assigns compact identifiers and key requirements to these methods.

sections.title: Content Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC defines three authenticated-encryption families: AES-GCM, AES-CCM, and ChaCha20/Poly1305. AES-GCM uses a 96-bit nonce and a 128-bit authentication tag. AES-CCM offers combinations of length-field size, tag size, and key size; the RFC defines eight algorithm identifiers. ChaCha20/Poly1305 uses a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce.

Key-and-nonce pairs must be unique for each encrypted message. The RFC also sets usage limits for algorithms, including a maximum of 2^32 AES-GCM messages under one key and a maximum of 2^61 AES block-cipher operations for AES-CCM.
sections.plainLanguage: These encryption methods also detect changes to encrypted messages. Each message needs a unique key-and-nonce pair, and the algorithms have limits on how often a key can be used.

sections.title: Deriving and Distributing Keys
sections.content:
HKDF turns a shared secret into key material and uses context information to bind the result to its intended use. The context includes an algorithm identifier, information about the sender and receiver, the requested key length, and optional public or private data. The RFC defines HMAC-based and AES-MAC-based HKDF variants.

COSE can distribute content keys directly, derive them from a shared secret, wrap them with AES Key Wrap, or derive them using ECDH. ECDH may use ephemeral-static or static-static keys and is followed by HKDF. COSE does not define an ephemeral-ephemeral mode because it is not itself an online protocol for establishing ephemeral secrets on both sides.
sections.plainLanguage: Two parties can derive a content key from a shared secret and context, or one key can protect another key for transfer. The context helps ensure that derived keys differ by purpose and direction.

sections.title: Key Objects and Encoding Rules
sections.content:
The document defines COSE key types for Octet Key Pair (OKP), elliptic-curve keys with x and y coordinates (EC2), and symmetric keys. Key parameters identify curves and contain public or private key material. Applications must check that the key type and curve are consistent.

The RFC also defines capability descriptions for algorithms and keys, so devices can describe supported combinations. COSE_KDF_Context encodings must use definite lengths and the shortest possible argument encoding. Applications must not generate or process maps with the same label used twice.
sections.plainLanguage: A COSE key object labels the kind of key and carries the parameters needed to use it. Devices can describe their supported algorithms and key types, and encodings must avoid duplicate map labels.

sections.title: Key Use and Trust
sections.content:
Implementations must protect private key material and should restrict each key to one algorithm. They must check that key type, algorithm, and operation match. The RFC notes that some algorithms limit how many times a key can be used and that nonce values must meet their algorithm's uniqueness requirements.

Before using a key or acting on received information, an application needs a trust decision about the key and its owner's permissions. COSE does not provide a uniform message-padding method, so applications may need their own padding rules to reduce information revealed by message lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect private keys and do not reuse one key across different algorithms. Applications must also decide whether a key and its owner's request are trusted in the current context.
